# Logging, errors, privacy, and audit

- Log security-relevant events and privileged state changes with timestamp, actor/service identity, action, target reference, outcome, trusted source context, and correlation ID.
- Never log passwords, private keys, bearer/session/reset tokens, authorization headers, full payment data, or secret values. Mask or tokenize personal and account data according to classification.
- Treat log data as untrusted. Use structured logging fields instead of constructing log lines from raw input; neutralize line breaks when a plain-text sink is unavoidable.
- Separate user-facing errors from internal diagnostics. Return a stable error code and safe message; keep stack traces, queries, internal hosts/paths, and upstream bodies out of responses.
- Do not disclose whether an account, tenant, object, or secret exists when that fact is sensitive. Keep body, status, headers, and materially different timing consistent where practical.
- Preserve the original exception and correlation when wrapping errors, but do not catch broadly and continue in an insecure or partially committed state.
- Make audit records append-oriented and protect access/integrity. Record authorization denials and administrative changes without turning expected invalid input into alert noise.
- Minimize personal data collection and retention. Keep telemetry purpose-specific, avoid high-cardinality sensitive labels, and honor deletion/retention requirements across logs and backups.
- Do not send sensitive data to analytics, crash reporting, tracing, or third-party observability by default. Apply centralized redaction before export.
- Ensure logging failure cannot reveal secrets or bypass a security decision. Avoid synchronous unbounded logging on attacker-controlled high-volume paths.
